title: Àlọ́ ÌJÀPÁ
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Àlọ́ kì í dákẹ́ láì sọ̀rọ̀ Ìjàpá; ọlọ́gbọ́n kì í dákẹ́ láì gbọ́n. (The folktale never finishes without the tortoise; the wise man never remains silent without wisdom: The tortoise symbolizes the duality of human intellect—cunning ingenuity must be tempered by communal ethics).
antiquity_timeline: Rooted in oral traditions of the Ọ̀yọ́ and Ifẹ̀ kingdoms before the 16th century; universal moral pedagogy across all Yorùbá homesteads.
provenance_and_citations: Babalọlá, Adébóyè (1966). The Content and Form of Yoruba Ijala. Oxford: Clarendon Press; Finnegan, Ruth (2012). Oral Literature in Africa. Cambridge: Open Book Publishers; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa. Bloomington: Indiana University Press.

title: Oríkì
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Oríkì ni ń mú ọmọ Ọba yangàn; bí a bá kì ẹnìkan, orí rẹ̀ a wú. (Panegyric praise elevates the prince to dignity; when one's oríkì is chanted, their spiritual head swells with divine grace: Oríkì activates the ontological essence of a person's inner destiny, aligning them with ancestral valor).
antiquity_timeline: Classical Ifẹ̀ (c. 11th–14th century) royal court recitations by palace bards (Àrọ̀kìn); institutionalized in Old Ọ̀yọ́ Empire with Dùndún talking drum syllabic transposition; preserved in transatlantic diaspora as sacred lucumí chants.
provenance_and_citations: Barber, Karin (1991). I Could Speak Until Tomorrow: Oriki, Women, and the Past in a Yoruba Town. Edinburgh University Press; Olatunji, Olatunde O. (1984). Features of Yoruba Oral Poetry. Ibadan: University Press PLC; Johnson, Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas. London: Routledge.

title: Ìyẹ̀rẹ̀ Ifá
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀rọ̀ tí a bá ń kọ ní Ìyẹ̀rẹ̀ Ifá kì í bọ́ sọ́nà; ẹnu àwọn Babaláwo ni ìmọ̀ wà. (The sacred verse chanted in Ìyẹ̀rẹ̀ Ifá never falls astray on the roadside; wisdom abides securely in the mouth of the initiated priests: The rhythmic cadence of Ìyẹ̀rẹ̀ Ifá preserves the 256 Odù from corruption or human alteration).
antiquity_timeline: Ancient Ifẹ̀ priesthood oral codification; formalized during the rise of the Ọ̀yọ́ royal divination college; modern preservation in UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage registry (2005).
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus. Ibadan: Oxford University Press Nigeria; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa. Indiana University Press; Verger, Pierre Fatumbi (1995). Ewé: The Use of Plants in Yoruba Society. São Paulo: Odebrecht.

title: Ewì
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ewì lẹṣin ọ̀rọ̀ àti àkọsílẹ̀ ọkàn; bí ọ̀rọ̀ bá sọnù, ewì la fi ń wá a. (Poetry is the steed of language and the inscription of the heart; when meaning is lost, poetry is the sacred vessel dispatched to retrieve it: Ewì elevates everyday vernacular into elevated philosophical dialectic).
antiquity_timeline: Classical oral verse tradition; modern renaissance pioneered by Oládẹ̀jọ Òkédìjí, Adébáyọ̀ Fálétí, and Tubọ̀sún Ọládàpọ̀ through radio, vinyl recordings, and print in the 20th century.
provenance_and_citations: Olatunji, Olatunde O. (1984). Features of Yoruba Oral Poetry. Ibadan: University Press PLC; Fálétí, Adébáyọ̀ (1982). Ewì Ìwòyí. Longman Nigeria; Barber, Karin (2000). The Generation of Plays: Yoruba Popular Life in Theater. Indiana University Press.

title: Àlọ́ Àmoṣùn
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Àlọ́ mi dọ̀bọ̀rọ̀ kò lẹ́sẹ̀ kò lọ́wọ́; ọgbọ́n orí ni a fi ń mọ̀ ọ́n. (My riddle is smooth without feet or hands; only the discernment of the mind unravels it: Riddles test epistemological agility and cognitive sharpness in youth).
antiquity_timeline: Primordial communal twilight hearth tradition across all Yorùbá sub-groups; foundational pedagogical device preceding formal initiation into adult guilds.
provenance_and_citations: Babalọlá, Adébóyè (1975). Àkójọpọ̀ Àlọ́ Ìjàpá. Oxford University Press; Bascom, William (1975). African Dilemma Tales. The Hague: Mouton; Finnegan, Ruth (2012). Oral Literature in Africa. Cambridge.

title: Rárà
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Rárà kì í ṣe orin àfowófa; ọ̀rọ̀ ìjìnlẹ̀ àtijọ́ ni akọrárà ń kọ. (Rárà chanting is not frivolous entertainment; the minstrel delivers the deep, unvarnished chronicles of antiquity: Itinerant bards preserve lineage secrets that written records omit).
antiquity_timeline: Archaic lineage chant form cultivated in Ọ̀yọ́, Ìbàdàn, and Ẹ̀gbá courts; sung by itinerant bards (akọrárà) to recount family epics and heroic exploits.
provenance_and_citations: Olatunji, Olatunde O. (1984). Features of Yoruba Oral Poetry. Ibadan: University Press PLC; Babalọlá, Adébóyè (1966). The Content and Form of Yoruba Ijala. Oxford: Clarendon Press.

title: Ẹ̀ṣà Ẹégún
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ẹ̀ṣà Ẹégún kì í purọ́; ohùn àwọn baba wa tó ti kọjá ni. (The ancestral masquerade chant never speaks falsehood; it is the living voice of our departed forebears: Masqueraders transcend mortal subjectivity to deliver divine ancestral judgment).
antiquity_timeline: Rooted in the ancient Egúngún mysteries of Old Ọ̀yọ́ and Nupe/Tapa borderlands; sung by the Oloojé guild with guttural vocal alteration (ohùn igi).
provenance_and_citations: Babayemi, S. O. (1980). Egungun Among the Oyo Yoruba. Ibadan: Board Publications; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gẹ̀lẹ̀dẹ́ Spectacle. University of Washington Press; Drewal, Henry John (1978). More Powerful Than Each Other: An Egbado Classification of Egungun. African Arts.

title: Ofo
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ofò kì í já mọ́ asán; àṣẹ tó wà lẹ́nu Babaláwo ni ń mú ọ̀rọ̀ ṣẹ. (The sacred incantation never returns void; the àṣẹ abiding in the diviner's mouth brings the metaphysical reality to pass: Words are vibrational instruments possessing physical potency).
antiquity_timeline: Pre-dynastic metaphysical science of àṣẹ; practiced by medicinal guilds (Ọlọ́ṣanyìn) and Ifá initiates; preserved in ancient esoteric formularies.
provenance_and_citations: Verger, Pierre Fatumbi (1995). Ewé: The Use of Plants in Yoruba Society. São Paulo: Odebrecht; Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1977). Àwọn Ojú Odù Mẹ́rìndínlógún. Oxford University Press; Buckley, Anthony D. (1985). Yoruba Medicine. Oxford: Clarendon Press.

title: Àró
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Àró kì í gba aṣọ tó dọ̀tí; ìwà mímọ́ ni ń bẹ nínú agbada aró. (The indigo dye vat never accepts soiled cloth; purity and careful reverence dwell inside the vat: Indigo dyeing is a sacred chemical covenant governed by female guild divinities).
antiquity_timeline: Ancient textile guild technology dated to classical Ifẹ̀ and Ọ̀ṣọ́gbó; managed predominantly by elder women guilds (Ìyá Àró) using Lonchocarpus cyanescens fermentation.
provenance_and_citations: Wenger, Susanne (1983). The Sacred Groves of Oshogbo. Merz; Wolff, Norma H. (1982). Traditional Yoruba Textile Production. African Arts; Eicher, Joanne B. (1976). Nigerian Handcrafted Textiles. University of Ife Press.

title: Ìgálà
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìgálà kì í yàgò fún ọdẹ tó gbé ọkọ̀; agbára ogun ni ń pa ààlà. (The frontier warrior does not yield to the spear-bearer; martial vigilance defines the boundary: Borderland regions forged intense intercultural and military resilience).
antiquity_timeline: Medieval frontier interactions between eastern Yorùbá kingdoms and the Igala Kingdom across the Niger confluence (c. 15th–18th century).
provenance_and_citations: Boston, John S. (1968). The Igala Kingdom. Oxford University Press; Johnson, Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas. London: Routledge; Smith, Robert S. (1988). Warfare and Diplomacy in Pre-Colonial West Africa. University of Wisconsin Press.

title: Ẹ̀kún Ìyàwó
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ẹ̀kún Ìyàwó kì í ṣe ti ìbànújẹ́; omijé ayọ̀ àti ìbà fún àwọn tó tọ́ ni dàgbà ni. (The nuptial lament is not born of sorrow; it is tears of filial reverence and joy thanking those who nurtured the bride: A sacred ritual transition from maidenhood to lineage matriarch).
antiquity_timeline: Archaic patrilocal marriage rites across all Yorùbá lands; performed on the eve of the bride's procession to her husband's compound.
provenance_and_citations: Olatunji, Olatunde O. (1984). Features of Yoruba Oral Poetry. Ibadan: University Press PLC; Barber, Karin (1991). I Could Speak Until Tomorrow. Edinburgh University Press; Fadipe, N. A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba. Ibadan University Press.

title: Orin Àárọ̀
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Orin àárọ̀ lẹgbẹ́ ń kọ sí oko; iṣẹ́ l'oògùn ìṣẹ́. (Morning song accompanies the farm guild to the fields; diligent labor is the sovereign antidote to poverty: Communal song synchronizes agricultural labor and banishes exhaustion).
antiquity_timeline: Agrarian cooperative labour guild (àáró and ọ̀wẹ̀) tradition established during the rise of permanent forest settlements.
provenance_and_citations: Fadipe, N. A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba. Ibadan University Press; Clarke, William H. (1972). Travels and Explorations in Yorubaland (1854-1858). Ibadan University Press.

title: Èfé
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Èfé kì í bẹ̀rù ọba; otitọ́ inú ni ń jáde lẹ́nu akẹ́fẹ́. (The satirical minstrel fears no monarch; unadorned truth flows from the mouth of the singer: Ritual satire functions as an inviolable democratic check against royal tyranny).
antiquity_timeline: Institutionalized nocturnal song performance within Gẹ̀lẹ̀dẹ́ masquerade societies among Southwestern (Kétu, Ẹ̀gbádò) Yorùbá since the 18th century.
provenance_and_citations: Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gẹ̀lẹ̀dẹ́ Spectacle: Art, Gender, and Social Harmony in an African Culture. Seattle: University of Washington Press; Drewal, Margaret Thompson (1992). Yoruba Ritual: Performers, Play, Agency. Indiana University Press.

title: Àrokò
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Àrokò kò gbọ́dọ̀ purọ́; ohun tí ojú rí ni ẹnu ń sọ, ohun tí ọwọ́ rán ni àrokò ń jẹ́. (The symbolic messenger must not distort the truth; what the eyes saw is spoken, what the sender bound is what the token proclaims: Mnemonic cryptography communicated war, peace, and covenant without written script).
antiquity_timeline: Pre-colonial cryptographic diplomatic system used across the Ọ̀yọ́, Ẹ̀gbá, and Ìjẹ̀bú kingdoms for interstate communications and secret guild directives.
provenance_and_citations: Johnson, Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas. London: Routledge; Bloxam, G. W. (1887). West African Symbolic Messages. Journal of the Anthropological Institute; Oduyoye, Modupe (1971). The Vocabulary of Yoruba Religious Discourse. Daystar Press.

title: Orin Ọba
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Orin Ọba kì í kùnà lẹ́nu àwọn Akínyẹlé; adé orí Ọba ni ń bùkún orin. (The royal anthem never stumbles on the lips of court chanters; the sacred crown on the king's head sanctifies the song: Palace music reinforces the divine right and cosmic legitimacy of the Aláàfin).
antiquity_timeline: Formalized court protocol of the Ọ̀yọ́ Palace (Àfin Aláàfin) and classical Ifẹ̀ monarchies; performed by specialized lineages of royal bards.
provenance_and_citations: Johnson, Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas. London: Routledge; Waterman, Christopher A. (1990). Jùjú: A Social History and Ethnography of an African Popular Music. University of Chicago Press; Euba, Akin (1990). Yoruba Drumming: The Dundun Tradition. Bayreuth African Studies.

title: Àwọn Owe Àgbà
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Òwe lẹṣin ọ̀rọ̀, bí ọ̀rọ̀ bá sọnù, òwe la fi ń wá a. (The proverb is the horse of speech; when the word is lost, the proverb is the instrument deployed to recover it: Elders communicate multi-layered judicial and moral precedent through parabolic brevity).
antiquity_timeline: Primordial philosophical corpus of the Yorùbá civilization; serving as the unwritten common law, ethical guide, and epistemological bedrock of all council deliberations.
provenance_and_citations: Owomoyela, Oyekan (2005). Yoruba Proverbs. University of Nebraska Press; Delano, Isaac O. (1966). Owe l'Esin Oro: Yoruba Proverbs—Their Meaning and Usage. Oxford University Press; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination. Indiana University Press.

title: Ìtàn Àdáyébá
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìtàn àdáyébá ni gbòǹgbò orílẹ̀-èdè; igi tí kò ní gbòǹgbò kì í dúró nígbà tí ìjì bá dé. (Ancient mythic history is the taproot of the nation; a tree without roots cannot withstand the arrival of the storm: Cosmogonic memory grounds human identity in divine origins).
antiquity_timeline: Primordial creation narratives centered on Ilé-Ifẹ̀ as the cradle of humankind; codified across generations through sacred royal genealogies and temple rites.
provenance_and_citations: Idowu, E. Bolaji (1962). Olodumare: God in Yoruba Belief. London: Longmans; Johnson, Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas. London: Routledge; Frobenius, Leo (1913). The Voice of Africa. London: Hutchinson.

title: Orin Ọ̀ṣun
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Orin Ọ̀ṣun lomi ń mú wá; ẹlẹ́rò tó ń pèsè ọmọ fún àgàn. (The hymn of Ọ̀ṣun brings soothing waters; the benevolent divinity who gifts children to the barren: Melodic chants accompanied by bronze bells celebrate maternal grace and sweet abundance).
antiquity_timeline: Ritual liturgies preserved by the Ataoja of Ọ̀ṣọgbó and the Ìyá Ọ̀ṣun priesthood at the Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove (UNESCO World Heritage Site).
provenance_and_citations: Murphy, Joseph M. and Sanford, Mei-Mei (2001). Osun Across the Waters: A Yoruba Goddess in Africa and the Americas. Indiana University Press; Wenger, Susanne (1983). The Sacred Groves of Oshogbo. Merz.

title: Èsè Ifá
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Èsè Ifá kọ́ wa ní ìtọjú orí; ìmọ̀ àtọ̀runwá kì í parọ́. (The verses of Ifá instruct us in the preservation of the inner head; celestial wisdom never speaks falsehood: Every stanza contains ontological diagnosis and pragmatic ethical guidance).
antiquity_timeline: Canonical oral encyclopedic verses structured across the 256 Odù Ifá; recognized as masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in 2005.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá. UNESCO; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa. Indiana University Press; Epega, A. A. and Neimark, Philip John (1995). The Sacred Ifa Oracle. HarperOne.

title: Orin Ìṣẹ́gún
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Orin ìṣẹ́gún ni a fi ń dágun mọ́; ogun parí, orin ayọ̀ bẹ̀rẹ̀. (The victory song marks the resolution of war; the conflict ceases, and the chorus of collective joy commences: Celebrates communal survival, heroic martial resolve, and restoration of peace).
antiquity_timeline: Military anthem genre sung by returning warrior assemblies (Ẹ̀gbẹ́ Ọdẹ and Balógun cavalry) during 18th- and 19th-century Yorùbá resistance campaigns.
provenance_and_citations: Smith, Robert S. (1988). Warfare and Diplomacy in Pre-Colonial West Africa. University of Wisconsin Press; Johnson, Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas. London: Routledge; Akintoye, S. A. (1971). Revolution and Power Politics in Yorubaland 1840-1893. Longman.

title: Àkàpò
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Àkàpò ló mọ orí Ifá; ẹni tí kò bọ̀wọ̀ fún àkàpò kò lè kọ́ ìmọ̀ ìjìnlẹ̀. (The apprentice holds the threshold of divine wisdom; he who fails to honor the bag-bearer cannot attain sacred mastery: Humility and service precede prophetic insight).
antiquity_timeline: Traditional pedagogical apprenticeship system of the Ifá priesthood (Ẹ̀kọ́ Ifá) dating to primordial Ifẹ̀; lasting 10 to 16 years under a master Babaláwo.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus. Ibadan: Oxford University Press Nigeria; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination. Indiana University Press.

title: Orin Ọmọ
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Orin ọmọ ni ń dẹ́kùn ẹkún; ọmọ làwùjọ ẹ̀dá, ọmọ làkọ́kọ́ nínú ohun gbogbo. (The lullaby soothes the weeping child; children are the crown of existence, children are paramount above all treasures: Lullabies bond maternal frequencies to the newborn's nascent consciousness).
antiquity_timeline: Domestic maternal oral tradition cultivated by mothers and grandmothers across compound courtyards throughout centuries of West African history.
provenance_and_citations: Olatunji, Olatunde O. (1984). Features of Yoruba Oral Poetry. Ibadan: University Press PLC; Fadipe, N. A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba. Ibadan University Press.

title: Èjì Ogbè
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Èjì Ogbè ni baba àwọn Odù; a kì í rí ojú Ogbè ká tún fojú sẹ́kún. (Èjì Ogbè is the royal patriarch of all 256 Odù; one never beholds the face of Ogbè and remains in tears: Embodies unclouded solar illumination, universal harmony, and sovereign prosperity).
antiquity_timeline: First and paramount sign of the 16 Principal Olódù Ifá; cosmological archetype of creation, dawn, and benevolent sovereignty across ancient West Africa and the transatlantic world.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá. UNESCO; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination. Indiana University Press; Fatunmbi, Awo Falokun (1992). Iwa-pele: Ifa Quest. Original Publications.

title: Ọ̀yá
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀yá tó l'ẹ́fúùfù lẹ́yìn; ẹlẹ́rù tí ń gbé igi gbòǹgbò. (Ọ̀yá who commands the tempest in her wake; the fearsome divinity who uproots ancient trees: Orisha of winds, hurricanes, river Niger, and the guardian gateway between mortals and ancestors).
antiquity_timeline: Primordial river divinity and royal consort of Ṣàngó in Classical Old Ọ̀yọ́; worshipped across West Africa (Odò Ọya), Brazil (Iansã), and Cuba (Oyá Yansa).
provenance_and_citations: Gleason, Judith (1987). Oya: In Praise of the Goddess. Boston: Shambhala; Verger, Pierre Fatumbi (1957). Notes sur le culte des orisa et vodun. Dakar: IFAN; Idowu, E. Bolaji (1962). Olodumare: God in Yoruba Belief. Longmans.

title: Yemọja
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Yemọja olómi tútù; ìyá tó gbọ́ ti ọmọ rẹ̀ nínú ibú. (Yemọja, custodian of soothing living waters; the maternal mother who hears her children's cry from the deepest oceanic trench: Primordial mother of the orishas, embodiment of maternal protection and unmeasured abundance).
antiquity_timeline: Ancient river divinity of the Ògùn river in Yorùbáland; expanded through the Transatlantic passage into the universal queen of the ocean (Yemayá in Lucumí, Iemanjá in Candomblé).
provenance_and_citations: Barnes, Sandra T. (1997). Africa's Ogun: Old World and New. Indiana University Press; Verger, Pierre Fatumbi (1957). Notes sur le culte des orisa et vodun. Dakar: IFAN; Thompson, Robert Farris (1983). Flash of the Spirit: African and Afro-American Art and Philosophy. New York: Vintage Books.
